subject: Accounting
title: Correcting Entries
description: A quick win: understand Correcting Entries.

hook.text: You posted $500 to office supplies. It should have been repairs. Time for a correcting entry.

buildup.text: Correcting entries fix errors discovered after the original entry was posted.

discovery.text: You reverse the wrong entry and record the right one—restoring the books to their correct state.

twist.text: Never erase or delete an original entry. The correction itself becomes part of the permanent record.

climax.text: A clear audit trail of corrections shows transparency—hiding fixes raises red flags.

punchline.text: Mistakes happen. Transparent corrections build trust.

quiz.question: How should bookkeeping errors be fixed?
options: With a correcting entry that reverses the error
By ignoring it if the amount is small

details.summary: Correcting entries fix errors discovered in previously recorded journal entries. This topic covers how to identify common bookkeeping mistakes and the proper techniques for correcting them without creating a bigger mess.
details.whyItMatters: Errors happen in every set of books. Knowing how to correct them properly—rather than just deleting or overwriting—maintains a reliable audit trail and keeps financial statements accurate.
takeaways: Never erase or delete an erroneous entry; record a correcting entry to reverse it
Common errors include wrong amounts, wrong accounts, and entries in the wrong period
Correcting entries should include a clear explanation referencing the original mistake

faq.question: How do you correct a bookkeeping error?
faq.answer: Record a correcting journal entry that reverses the incorrect entry and then record the correct entry. Never simply delete the original—this destroys the audit trail. Include a memo explaining the error and referencing the original entry number.

faq.question: What are the most common bookkeeping errors?
faq.answer: Common errors include transposition errors (writing 540 instead of 450), posting to the wrong account, recording the wrong amount, omitting transactions entirely, and recording entries in the wrong accounting period. Regular reconciliation catches most of these.
